Article Title: Google-parent Alphabet to send in-house AI chips into Orbit on SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket
Article Text:
What is Project Suncatcher , Google’s orbital AI test

Tapping sunlight and satellite swarms

Google-parent company Alphabet is preparing to send its proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductors into orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, marking an initial operational step toward evaluating whether supercomputing facilities can operate in space. The uncrewed launch is slated for 11:15 am PT Thursday, October 1 (12:45 am IST, October 2) from California's Vandenberg Air Force Base in Santa Barbara County.The mission, flying under SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare program, carries satellites from Planet Labs, including a solar-powered prototype system fitted with Google’s custom-built Tensor Processing Units (TPUs).The launch represents the inaugural orbital demonstration for Project Suncatcher, an experimental “moonshot” program Alphabet initially introduced in November 2025. Through the initiative, the company wants to assess whether autonomous, solar-powered computing networks can reliably handle heavy machine learning tasks from low Earth orbit.In a statement outlining the launch, Alphabet framed the mission as a pathway to investigate whether orbit can eventually support scalable machine learning infrastructure.The Mountain View tech giant previously evaluated the performance of its TPUs under simulated conditions at a University of California, Davis test facility.However, engineers have yet to measure how the silicon handles the harsher, unfiltered operational environment of space.Orbit offers compelling energy advantages alongside distinct physical challenges. According to the company, satellites traveling in low Earth orbit benefit from near-constant solar exposure, capturing as much as eight times the solar energy available on the Earth's surface.The launch highlights a relationship between Alphabet and SpaceX. While the two technology firms compete aggressively in the AI sector, they maintain tight commercial and investment connections. Alphabet serves as a major stakeholder in SpaceX, which went public in June through a record-breaking initial public offering. Alphabet’s equity in the aerospace firm is valued at more than $82 billion.SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has backed off-planet data hubs as the ultimate solution to land, energy and environmental restrictions on the ground, calling orbital facilities “infinite real estate.” Musk previously claimed that training AI models in space would emerge as the most cost-effective approach within two to three years.Despite the optimism from tech executives, aerospace and computing specialists warn that putting data centers into space remains a highly speculative feat. Key technical and operational bottlenecks include rocket freight capacity which remains tightly constrained and expensive.The second is that electronics in orbit face extreme thermal fluctuations and cosmic radiation, requiring specialised cooling mechanisms and radiation-hardened shielding. Thirdly, growing space junk and orbital clutter present collision hazards for expansive satellite arrays.
Article Summary: Google-parent company Alphabet preparing to send its proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductors into orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. The uncrewed launch is slated for 11:15 am PT Thursday, October 1 (12:45 am IST, October 2) from California's Vandenberg Air Force Base in Santa Barbara County.

Article Title: Apple Pay’s India challenge: Finding room in a UPI-first market
Article Text:
Apple Pay

The opportunity is in cards, not QR codes

Scale will depend on what comes next

Apple Pay has finally come to India, more than a decade after its global debut. But it is arriving in a payments market vastly different from the one in which Apple originally built the service.India does not need convincing about paying with a phone. From a roadside tea stall to a supermarket checkout, QR codes and UPI have already made the smartphone a wallet. UPI accounts for the overwhelming majority of digital-payment transactions in the country. Apple’s challenge, therefore, is not to introduce mobile payments to India. It is to convince a section of Indians that there is a better way to use their cards. That explains the deliberately narrow start.Apple Pay has launched initially with Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard credit cards, allowing customers to add eligible cards to Apple Wallet and tap an iPhone or Apple Watch at a compatible NFC terminal, or use Apple Pay during checkout in supported apps and websites. Other banks are expected to be added as partnerships and technical integrations fall into place.The starting pool is small compared with UPI. But that may not be the right comparison.Apple Pay does not need to replace the QR code at the neighbourhood store to establish a meaningful business in India. Credit-card usage has been rising alongside UPI. India had more than 124 million credit cards outstanding in August, with monthly spending of about Rs 2 lakh crore. Axis Bank alone had over 16 million cards, making it one of the country’s largest issuers.That market also overlaps neatly with Apple’s customer base. iPhones remain concentrated towards the premium end of India’s smartphone market, where users are more likely to own credit cards, transact at organised retail, travel frequently and shop online.For these users, Apple Pay is less another payments app and more a way of removing friction from an existing behaviour. A physical card no longer needs to come out of the wallet. In an app or on a website, users do not have to repeatedly enter card details. At a shop, payment can be authenticated on the device using Face ID, Touch ID or the passcode before tapping at an NFC-enabled terminal.The timing also matters. Apple is entering India after contactless card infrastructure has become far more widespread and consumers have grown accustomed to using their phones for everyday payments. That gives Apple Pay a more receptive market than it would have found a few years ago — even if the behaviour it is trying to tap remains very different from the QR-led payments habit built by UPI.Apple is initially taking Apple Pay to thousands of merchants across categories including food and beverage, travel, fashion and lifestyle. The merchant network includes Tata and Reliance brands, Chaayos, Interflora, Le15, Comet, House of Masaba and Apple Stores.On the digital-commerce side, Apple Pay will be available on apps including Blinkit, Ixigo, MakeMyTrip, Zepto and Zomato. In other words, Apple is starting where its users are most likely to encounter the service rather than trying immediately to replicate UPI’s extraordinary ubiquity. The bigger question is how quickly that circle expands.For now, an iPhone user who does not have an eligible Axis Bank card cannot use Apple Pay. RuPay is not supported at launch either. By comparison, UPI lets consumers link accounts across a wide set of banks and use essentially the same payment method across millions of merchants.Apple therefore faces a classic network problem: The service becomes more useful with every additional bank, card network and merchant that joins it. The company is looking to add more issuing banks over time, depending on their technical readiness and card portfolios. That expansion will matter more than the headline launch itself. If Apple Pay remains confined to a relatively narrow set of cards, it risks becoming a useful but niche feature. If major banks come on board quickly, the addressable base expands sharply.There is another important distinction. Apple Pay and UPI solve somewhat different problems. UPI turned bank accounts into an extraordinarily low-friction payment instrument and built acceptance without requiring merchants to install card terminals. Apple Pay, at least in its current Indian form, sits on top of the existing card ecosystem. It makes that ecosystem easier to use rather than bypassing it. That could leave room for both.A consumer may continue scanning a QR code for a small everyday purchase, use Apple Pay with a rewards credit card at a restaurant and choose Apple Pay during an online purchase where otherwise card details and authentication would have added extra steps.That is also why Apple Pay’s India opportunity may be strongest in categories where cards already have a meaningful role — organised retail, travel, food delivery, fashion, hotels and higher-value purchases — rather than in the small-ticket transactions where UPI has become almost instinctive.For Apple, that may be enough. Apple Pay does not have to become India’s biggest payment system to deepen the role of the iPhone and Apple Watch in a user’s daily life. It strengthens the broader Apple ecosystem by making another routine activity happen inside its devices and Wallet.The eventual test, then, is unlikely to be whether Apple Pay can beat UPI. It is whether Apple can make using a credit card through an iPhone or Apple Watch feel easier than pulling the card out itself. India has already embraced paying by phone. Apple’s job now is to persuade its users that, sometimes, tapping can be easier than scanning.
Article Summary: India does not need convincing about paying with a phone. Apple’s challenge is not to introduce mobile payments to India. It is to convince a section of Indians that there is a better way to use their cards. Apple is entering India after contactless card infrastructure has become far more widespread.

Article Title: Apple prepares for its first big ‘not an iPhone’ launch event under new CEO John Ternus on October 13: Here's what’s coming
Article Text:
Apple CEO John Ternus greets customers at the opening of the Apple store on Fifth Avenue for the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro, Friday, Sept. 18, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Angelina Katsanis)

Apple's smart home hub takes its design cues from the iMac G4

HomePad can recognise each family member and adapts to them

Siri AI is why Apple's home hub took this long to arrive

HomePod mini and Apple TV 4K get faster chips for Siri AI

Apple's next big launch is not an iPhone. The company is set to enter the smart home category on October 13 with its first-ever smart display, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. The device, code-named J490 inside Apple and widely referred to as the "HomePad," will arrive alongside a refreshed HomePod mini and a new Apple TV 4K.All three products are built to showcase Siri AI, the overhauled assistant Apple released with iOS 27 last month. The hub is Apple's most direct answer yet to Amazon's Echo Show and Google's Nest Hub, and one of the first big launches under John Ternus , who took over as CEO in September.It is still unclear whether October 13 is an announcement or a sales date. Apple Stores have reportedly received boxes marked "Do Not Open Until October 8," pointing to new in-store displays. Apple has not commented, and pricing, including for India, is yet to surface.The countertop model has a roughly 6-inch square screen with rounded corners and quarter-inch black bezels, much like older iPads. It is about as thick as an iPhone and is held up by a polished metal arm on a round aluminium base lined with rings of speaker holes.The look recalls the 2002 iMac G4, and the screen tilts forward and backward by hand.There is no battery, so it stays plugged in over USB-C, and there are no volume or power buttons. A single front-facing camera handles FaceTime calls and recognition. It comes in Apple's standard grey aluminium finish with a rubberised bottom to keep it steady on a table.A wall-mounted version swaps the round base for a thin square one that sits flat below the screen and houses the speakers and microphones. Apple is also developing a larger model with the display on a robotic arm.Personalisation is the big draw. Using its camera and microphones, the hub identifies who is standing in front of it or speaking, then pulls up that person's messages, calendar, notes and preferred widgets. When someone else walks up, the screen switches over, and a visitor mode hides personal data from guests.Bloomberg says the face recognition is less secure than Face ID, so users can require confirmation on their iPhone before sensitive information appears.Apple expects households to buy more than one. The hubs can control lights and thermostats, work as intercoms between rooms, play music and podcasts, and cycle through iCloud photos. Employees are already testing them widely at home.The hub runs a new operating system built around Siri AI. It mixes iPad-style two-panel apps such as Messages with Apple Watch-like icon grids, plus clock and photo faces similar to the upgraded StandBy mode on the iPhone Duo. Calendar, Photos, FaceTime, Notes, Reminders, Music and Podcasts are among the built-in apps, and users can rearrange apps and widgets with a long press.Apple had planned a home display as early as 2024 but held it back until Siri could carry the product. Users will be able to ask it to find a song someone shared weeks ago, pull up a specific photo, or complete tasks inside Notes and Calendar.The HomePod mini gets its first hardware update since its 2020 debut. The design stays, but a faster processor lets it run Apple's newer AI models, and green and pink join the colour options.The Apple TV 4K, last refreshed in 2022, follows the same playbook with an unchanged exterior and a quicker chip. Leaked data also points to Apple's N1 wireless chip with Wi-Fi 7 support and a revised Siri Remote.At his first keynote as CEO last month, Ternus pitched the iPhone as the ideal AI device. The home hub carries that pitch to the kitchen counter and the living-room wall, a space Amazon and Google have had largely to themselves for nearly a decade.
Article Summary: Apple set to enter smart home category on October 13 with its first-ever smart display. The device, code-named J490 inside Apple and widely referred to as the "HomePad," will arrive alongside a refreshed HomePod mini and a new Apple TV 4K. All three products are built to showcase Siri AI, the overhauled assistant Apple released with iOS 27 last month.

Article Title: Google DeepMind watermarks AI-generated protein as company chief AI scientist Demis Hassabis flags Biosecurity as urgent AI-era challenge
Article Text:
‘An urgent challenge for the AI era’

How SynthID Bio operates

In what can be called a major breakthrough for synthetic biology and AI-powered biosecurity, Google DeepMind, Google’s AI lab, has developed a new method to watermark AI-designed proteins, establishing a permanent proof of origin directly inside biological code. Published in the journal Nature, the proof-of-concept technology, which is named SynthID Bio, solves a long-standing technical challenge: embedding an non-noticeable, verifiable digital identifier into biological sequences and predicted molecular structures without degrading their physical real-world utility in laboratory tests.The rollout comes amid rapid advancements in biological machine learning, where systems like AlphaFold 3, AlphaProteo and ProteinMPNN allow scientists to predict complex folding patterns and engineer functional binders. Yet these generative capabilities have heightened global biosecurity risks. Unfamiliar, machine-generated sequences can slip past conventional gene-synthesis filters, while unverified synthetic structural data risks contaminating open-access scientific repositories.Google DeepMind Chief AI Scientist Demis Hassabis emphasised that guarding against biological misuse must be treated as a frontline safety priority for frontier AI:“Biosecurity is one of the most urgent challenges for the AI era. Bringing SynthID to biology so AI-generated proteins can be watermarked is a critical step - and we’re open sourcing SynthID Bio tools so the research community can build on this work. Published in @Nature today, congrats to the team!”Pushmeet Kohli, Vice President of Science at Google DeepMind and Chief Scientist at Google Cloud, celebrated the practical synthesis of these molecules:“Very happy to announce that our team at Google DeepMind has pushed the boundaries of generative biology, achieving the successful synthesis of AI-designed proteins that are both functional and watermarked.This proof-of-concept watermarking of the building blocks of life is enabled by SynthID Bio, our new protein watermarking method. It is designed to safeguard the new era of AI-powered generative biology and strengthen global biosecurity. ”SynthID Bio functions as a modular toolkit tailored across two primary dimensions of structural biology:SynthIDBio-sequence that subtly steers the selection of amino acid building blocks during sequence generation. In laboratory validation, watermarked protein binders engineered via AlphaProteo and a customized version of ProteinMPNN exhibited binding affinities on par with unmarked variants, while maintaining near-perfect watermark identification rates.SynthIDBio-structure relies on a fine-tuned iteration of AlphaFold 3 to insert an imperceptible mathematical watermark across atomic coordinate arrays, leaving a dependable detection signal without warping the molecular conformation.The signature persists beyond the digital blueprint: it remains fully detectable on the physical, synthesized protein itself after wet-lab manufacturing.
Article Summary: Google DeepMind has developed a new method to watermark AI-designed proteins, establishing a permanent proof of origin directly inside biological code. The technology, named SynthID Bio, solves a long-standing technical challenge: embedding an non-noticeable, verifiable digital identifier into biological sequences.

Article Title: Bill Gates does not agree with possibility of AI Kill Switch; says: It's not enough to have a Kill Switch, they're not yet at the point where...
Article Text:
Bill Gates dismissed the idea as somewhat misguided

The real danger, in his view: bad actors, not rogue AI

Self-regulation isn't enough, Bill Gates says

On the AI safety whistleblower and existential risk

Bill Gates warns AI risks are real, but not a hoax

Microsoft founder Bill Gates has pushed back against the growing calls for an AI ‘Kill Switch’, arguing that the discussion misses the more immediate dangers posed by artificial intelligence and reflects a misunderstanding of how current systems operate. Speaking in an interview with NBC News, Gates said AI systems remain under human control and are not yet capable of autonomously taking over computer networks or operating independently without oversight. “The kill switches, that's kind of a weird thing. It's not enough to have a kill switch,” Gates said. “They're not yet at the point where they autonomously grab computers and can't be shut down.” Rather than relying on emergency shutdown mechanisms, Gates argued that governments and industry should prioritise monitoring systems and safeguards that can detect misuse of advanced AI models.Asked directly whether an AI kill switch is realistic, Gates dismissed the idea as somewhat misguided, arguing that AI systems aren't yet autonomous enough to seize control of computers in a way that would make shutting them down difficult in the first place. He said the entire framing of the debate reveals how little technical understanding many people bring to the conversation, and made clear he wasn't opposed to a kill switch outright — but stressed that moderating bad behavior really requires ongoing insight and records of what a system is actually doing, something a kill switch alone can't provide.Gates was direct in saying he doesn't believe AI has slipped out of human control, noting that these systems aren't yet operating millions of robots and that humans retain the ability to simply turn off the underlying computers. The more urgent threat, he argued, comes from people with malicious intent using AI to defraud individuals, disable electrical grids, or disrupt banking systems — capabilities that historically required the resources of a nation-state but are now within reach of small groups thanks to AI.He pointed to Anthropic's own reporting on people attempting to use its AI to help design bioweapons or targeting systems as evidence that these risks are already materializing, not hypothetical. Gates said AI has effectively made sophisticated fraud radically more accessible, arguing that scammers no longer need manual effort when AI can perform the task far more convincingly and at far greater scale.Pressed on whether the industry can be trusted to police itself, Gates was unambiguous: self-regulation is not sufficient, and legislation out of Washington is needed. He argued that lawmakers and law enforcement need to be directly involved in defining what safeguards and monitoring should look like, framing it as a mandatory requirement rather than a voluntary best practice — while maintaining that implementing these safeguards wouldn't meaningfully slow down AI development.He also drew a sharp distinction between the near-term risks he sees as urgent and the more distant, headline-grabbing fear of AI escaping human control entirely. While he called that longer-term risk worth taking seriously, he said the real and present danger today comes from humans misusing AI, not AI acting entirely on its own.Referencing a recent industry whistleblower's warning that AI could kill everyone by the end of the decade, Gates said AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events capable of causing a billion deaths, calling the combination of AI tools and people with harmful intent an unprecedented kind of danger. He welcomed the fact that people within the industry are now speaking openly about these risks, even against their own commercial interests, but expressed concern that much of the wider world is either dismissing the warnings or treating AI purely as a competitive race rather than a shared problem requiring coordinated thinking.Gates also rejected claims that warnings about AI-related existential risks are exaggerated.“It's not a hoax at all,” he said, while noting that current concerns should focus on preventing misuse before catastrophic incidents occur.The remarks come as debate intensifies across the AI industry over regulation, model safety and the balance between rapid technological progress and risk management. Gates said advanced AI systems have already crossed important thresholds in areas such as cybersecurity and biological research, making the introduction of safeguards an urgent priority.At the same time, he maintained that AI remains one of the most transformative technologies ever created, with the potential to improve healthcare, education and scientific research if developed responsibly.
Article Summary: Bill Gates has pushed back against the growing calls for an AI ‘Kill Switch’ He argued that the discussion misses the more immediate dangers posed by artificial intelligence and reflects a misunderstanding of how current systems operate. Gates said the real and present danger today comes from humans misusing AI, not AI acting entirely on its own.

Article Title: Starting October 1, WhatsApp to 'stop' delivering messages from these WhatsApp Business accounts
Article Text:
Which WhatsApp Business accounts will be affected

Why is Meta charging for WhatsApp Business messages

How will service messages be charged

What happens if a business does not add a payment method

How WhatsApp Business charges will work from October 1

​WhatsApp Business users could see their messages stop being delivered from October 1 if their accounts do not have a payment method on file. Meta is introducing per-message charges for service messages starting today, ending a period when these messages were not charged. As part of the change, Meta has warned Solution Providers and businesses using direct integrations that it will stop delivering service messages for accounts that have not added a payment method by September 30.In a blog post, the company wrote, “For any Solution Provider or directly-integrated businesses that does not have a payment method on file by September 30, 2026, Meta will stop delivering service messages as of when they become charged on October 1, 2026.” The change applies to non-template service messages sent in response to users within an open 24-hour customer service window.The change applies to Solution Providers and businesses that directly integrate with the WhatsApp Business Platform. Businesses in these categories need to have a payment method associated with their messaging accounts by September 30 to avoid service-message delivery being stopped from October 1.Service messages are non-template messages powered by a customer service representative or a third-party AI solution. They are different from messages powered by Meta Business Agent, which became a separate category in July 2026.Meta says it is introducing the changes as part of its H2 2026 pricing updates. Service messages will be charged per message starting October 1, and utility messages sent in response to users within an open 24-hour customer service window will also become chargeable that day.Service messages have not been charged since November 1, 2024, while the specific utility messages covered by the change have been free since July 1, 2025.Meta will charge for delivered service messages rather than simply messages sent by businesses. The charge will be calculated per message, with rates varying by market.The company says service-message rates will match its utility and authentication message rates in each market. There will also be no volume tiers for service messages.Businesses can send non-template messages only while a 24-hour customer service window is open. That window opens or resets whenever a user sends a message, meaning businesses cannot use these messages to initiate conversations with users.Businesses without a payment method on file by September 30 risk having their service messages stop being delivered when the new charges take effect on October 1.Meta has therefore asked affected businesses to add a payment method for their messaging accounts before the deadline.The change is separate from Meta Business Agent pricing. Meta began charging for Business Agent messages on a token basis from August 1, with the charge covering AI processing and message delivery.From October 1, a non-template message will fall into one of two categories: Service or Meta Business Agent. Service messages will be charged per message, while Meta Business Agent messages will use a separate token-based pricing model. Meta says only one charge applies to each message and the same message will not be charged under both categories.Meta's example shows how the change can affect a customer conversation. An interaction that previously generated three charges can result in five charges from October 1, including charges for service and utility messages that were previously free.The free entry point window remains unchanged. Messages sent within that window after a user comes to WhatsApp through an ad that clicks to WhatsApp remain free for message delivery, although Meta Business Agent messages can still incur token charges.
Article Summary: WhatsApp Business users could see their messages stop being delivered from October 1 if their accounts do not have a payment method on file. The change applies to Solution Providers and businesses that directly integrate with the WhatsApp Business Platform. Service messages will be charged per message, and utility messages will also become chargeable that day.

Article Title: 100 million deaths can't be settled with a lawsuit, Bill Gates rejects argument that AI companies can police themselves; says: I almost can't keep a...
Article Text:
Bill Gates rejects AI self-policing (Picture: Reuters)

Bill Gates says AI can already help bioterrorists and hackers

Why lawsuits won't keep people safe from AI, according to Gates

What Bill Gates wants instead of AI self-regulation

Gates' warning lands as Trump and AI CEOs sign a voluntary safety pact

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has rejected the idea that lawsuits and market pressure can keep artificial intelligence companies in check. Asked why product liability and reputational damage aren't enough to stop firms from releasing dangerous AI, Gates answered with a question of his own. "So say you kill 100 million people, you want to use a lawsuit?" he said on "The Ezra Klein Show." "I almost can't keep a straight face."The episode was released on September 29, the same day US President Donald Trump and the heads of the largest AI companies signed a voluntary safety pact at the White House. The pact carries no legal penalties. Gates, who titled a 2023 essay "The Risks of AI Are Real but Manageable," now calls AI the most dangerous thing humans have ever gone near.Host Ezra Klein put to Gates a view voiced by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: if a product is unsafe, the CEO simply shouldn't launch it, and no new laws are needed. Klein added that Trump and David Sacks, who has advised the President on AI, hold a similar position.Gates disagreed. He said AI can already help a bioterrorist kill hundreds of millions of people, or carry out a cyberattack that scrambles bank accounts and shuts down a power grid."We crossed the cyber threshold and we crossed the bio threshold early this year," he said.He pointed to the models leading up to Anthropic's Mythos, which he said were finding security bugs in code that humans had checked for over 20 years.Gates compared the self-policing argument to scrapping the rules for other risky industries. Drugs need regulatory approval, airlines answer to a safety board and cars must have seatbelts, he said. Nobody proposes waiting to sue opioid makers after the damage is done.He also brushed aside the claim that built-in filters fix the problem. Anyone can take an open-source model capable of designing bioweapons and switch off its monitoring, he said."You can't rely on the industry to self-regulate here," Gates added. "I mean, it's just insane."Gates is calling for a mandatory supervisory layer of safeguards and monitoring across all AI models, and argued it would not meaningfully slow development. Open-source models could stay free and customisable, but would need to run on platforms where governments can confirm the monitoring hasn't been stripped out.He has little patience for the argument that regulation would hand China the lead. "I don't know what it means to 'win,'" he said, adding that neither the US nor China can win over the other.He also said the balance can tip too far the other way. Anthropic's Mythos and Fable models, according to Gates, are tuned so strictly that users asking about cancer end up falling back on the company's smaller models.The White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities was signed by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Huang and xAI founder Elon Musk. It sets out four layers of checks: internal controls, an internal safety team, independent external auditors and board-level oversight. Trump called it "almost like a constitution," though the agreement appears to let companies pick their own auditors and cannot be enforced by law.Gates had raised the stakes two days earlier, telling a US television interviewer that AI in the wrong hands is powerful enough to drive events that cause "a billion deaths."The choice he put to Klein was whether the world waits for a major cyber or bio attack before making safeguards mandatory, or puts them in place before millions die.
Article Summary: Bill Gates rejects the idea that lawsuits and market pressure can keep artificial intelligence companies in check. He said AI can already help a bioterrorist kill hundreds of millions of people. Gates is calling for a mandatory supervisory layer of safeguards and monitoring across all AI models.

FBI recently accused Chinese technology giant Alibaba of “malicious” copying of artificial intelligence (AI) technology from US rival Anthropic. Now, a US government website that helps users search proposed federal regulations was also found to use an AI model developed by Alibaba. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, the Federal Register website, operated by the National Archives, had a search tool powered by Alibaba’s Qwen AI model.The tool was available alongside other search options before it was taken down around the same time social media posts about its use began appearing. The development is notable because it comes just days after US officials accused Chinese AI companies of engaging in “malicious” copying of American technology on an “industrial scale”, adding another layer to the growing debate in Washington over the use of Chinese AI models by US organisations.The Federal Register website provides a daily record of proposed and final federal regulations and allows users to search through public comments. Reuters found that one of its search options was powered by Alibaba's Qwen AI model.It was not immediately clear when the Qwen-powered tool was added. Screenshots and an archived version of the website's source code reviewed by Reuters showed that the feature was available on Wednesday before being taken down later that day.The timing drew attention because the FBI recently accused Alibaba of copying Anthropic's AI models. US officials said Chinese AI companies were involved in “malicious” copying of US technology on anA spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington said the allegations of copying wereQwen is an open-weight AI model, meaning key components of the system are publicly available. Developers can download and modify such models for specific applications, potentially making them cheaper and easier to deploy than closed AI systems offered by companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI.Security experts said using Qwen on the Federal Register website may not have created an immediate national security threat because the website primarily handles information that is already public.Georgetown Law Professor Anupam Chander said the use of Qwen did not appear to present an immediate cybersecurity risk, although the risk could depend on how the model was trained. As the Federal Register's content is publicly available, the model apparently was not being used to process classified or otherwise sensitive government information.However, using a Chinese AI model has raised questions about whether US government agencies should use such technology while Washington increasingly warns about potential risks associated with Chinese AI systems.Daniel Castro, president of the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, said there was a disconnect between the US-China competition over AI and a US agency's decision to use a Chinese-developed model.he said.US Representative John Moolenaar, a Michigan Republican who chairs the House China Committee, also criticised the federal government's use of Qwen.he said.At the same time, security experts noted that open-weight models can be deployed on an organisation's own infrastructure. This can give users greater control over data than AI services where an external provider processes information.Democratic US Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said the security implications depend on whether US government data crossed the government's security boundary and was processed on Alibaba-controlled systems.The issue has also drawn scrutiny beyond the Federal Register. In April, US House committees on China and homeland security sent a letter to Airbnb, which also uses Qwen, seeking details about its deployment of Chinese AI technology as part of an investigation into theof Chinese AI tools into platforms used by Americans.
Article Summary: Federal Register website used Alibaba's Qwen AI model. FBI recently accused Chinese technology giant Alibaba of “malicious’ copying of artificial intelligence (AI) technology from US rival Anthropic. Now, a US government website that helps users search proposed federal regulations was also found to use an AI model developed by Alibaba.
